prompt.context: North-South Pharma Co is a US-based pharmaceutical manufacturer. The company owns a plant in the United States that is active in serving US customers through pharmacies, and also owns an idle plant in South America.
prompt.question: 1. Forecast revenue for North-South Pharma Co (market sizing). 2. What should North-South Pharma Co do with its idle South American facility?

clarifying_info.q: How much revenue does North-South Pharma Co make per prescription?
What is North-South Pharma Co's current market share?
clarifying_info.a: Approximately 5% of the US prescription market

clarifying_info.q: What is the capacity of each facility?
clarifying_info.a: US plant capacity: 50 million units; South American plant capacity: 20 million units

exhibits.title: US vs. South America Cost and Profitability Comparison
exhibits.shows: A table comparing per-unit economics and total profitability for the US facility versus the South American facility, including revenue per unit, variable cost line items, contribution margin, fixed costs, capacity, and total profit.

framework: Compare costs and profitability across US facility vs. South American facility using a matrix: Fixed Costs (land, SG&A, marketing, PPE) vs. Variable Costs (labor, raw materials, transportation/shipping)
Identify key cost drivers: US has higher labor and materials costs; South America has cheaper labor/materials but high shipping costs to serve US customers
Assess capacity utilization: required production volume based on market sizing vs. each facility's capacity
Calculate contribution margin and total profit for each facility to determine viability
Evaluate strategic options for the idle South American facility: sell, repurpose, sublet, or activate for new market entry

questions.prompt: Part 1: Size the US prescription market and forecast revenue for North-South Pharma Co.
questions.guidance: Candidate should walk through a top-down market sizing using US population, share of people visiting doctors, prescriptions per patient, revenue per prescription, and North-South's market share. Candidate should state assumptions clearly and ask for any missing data points (e.g., revenue per prescription, market share).

math.setup: Top-down market sizing: US population → people getting prescriptions → total prescriptions/year → total market revenue → North-South revenue at 5% share
steps: 300M US population x 10% visiting doctor = 30M people receiving prescriptions
$300M x 5% market capture = $15M revenue opportunity for North-South
math.answer: $15M estimated annual revenue for North-South Pharma Co

questions.prompt: Part 2: Using Exhibit 1, analyze the profitability of the US facility versus the South American facility and draw conclusions.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate total contribution margin for each facility using the market-sized volume (30M units from Part 1), then subtract fixed costs to derive profit. Key insight: US facility is profitable; South American facility breaks even at best when serving US customers due to high transportation costs. Candidate should identify transportation as the key cost driver and recommend a course of action.

math.setup: Apply market-sized demand (30M units) to each facility's unit economics from Exhibit 1
steps: US: 30M units x $0.25 CM/unit = $7.5M contribution margin; $7.5M - $5M fixed costs = $2.5M profit
South America: 30M units x $0.20 CM/unit = $6M contribution margin; BUT SA capacity is only 20M units, so: 20M units x $0.20 = $4M contribution margin; $4M - $4M fixed costs = $0 profit (break-even)
Key driver: SA transportation cost of $0.20/unit vs. $0.05/unit in the US makes SA facility uncompetitive for serving US market
math.answer: US facility profit: $2.5M. South American facility profit: $0 (break-even). The SA facility is not viable for serving US customers at current transportation costs.

brainstorming.prompt: What else can North-South Pharma Co do with its South American facility at this point? (Follow-up: What would be the implications of keeping the facility and entering the South American pharmaceutical market?)

categories.name: Sell the facility
ideas: Sell as-is to a competitor or manufacturing company
Sell in pieces: equipment, materials, and land separately

categories.name: Repurpose the facility
ideas: Use as a training facility for workers from the US plant
Use as a sales or administrative office (though large facility may not be cost-efficient)

categories.name: Sublet
ideas: Sublet to a competitor or another manufacturing company to generate rental income

categories.name: Enter South American market
ideas: Get facility operational to manufacture and distribute pharmaceuticals for the South American market where transportation costs would be far lower
Prospect local hospitals and pharmacies as distribution partners

categories.name: Implications of SA market entry — Internal
ideas: Hire and train local sales, manufacturing, and distribution workforce
Build relationships with local distribution partners (medical product carriers)
Manage local inventory for regional distribution
Risk of diverting management attention from profitable US operations
Risk of damaging brand with US clients if US operations suffer

categories.name: Implications of SA market entry — External
ideas: Assess SA market size and demand for prescriptions
Understand SA healthcare landscape and prescription dynamics
Evaluate geopolitical environment: taxation, pharmaceutical regulations, corruption risks
Determine competitive landscape in South American pharma market

recommendation: Option A: Divest the South American facility — the facility breaks even when serving US customers and represents idle capital; selling it unlocks value and removes ongoing fixed cost burden

Option B: Activate the facility to enter the South American pharmaceutical market — transportation costs to serve US make the SA plant uncompetitive for US distribution, but serving a local SA market would eliminate the high shipping cost and potentially make the facility profitable
risks: Option A risks: low selling price in an emerging market; severance and morale costs from laying off any existing SA workforce; potential loss of strategic optionality in a growing market

Option B risks: high cost and complexity of entering an entirely new geographic market; regulatory and compliance hurdles in South America; risk of alienating or neglecting US clients and employees by expanding abroad
next_steps: Option A: Engage a South American real estate or industrial asset broker to identify potential buyers; work with an HR/human capital consultancy to manage employee transitions and minimize severance costs

Option B: Retain legal counsel to map pharmaceutical regulations and licensing requirements in South America; begin prospecting local hospitals and pharmacies; conduct a full SA market sizing to validate revenue opportunity
